<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
# Review of the 24-Month Follow-up: Varden County and a Halden Subset

This is a good follow-up. It answers the question the earlier documents left open, whether the gains last, using the strongest design available: randomised, record-based output, two hours measures, and two years. The headline result is a smaller but persistent gain of about 8.5–10% per hour in case-processing. That result is credible and well calibrated. Its corrections to Varga & Holm and to the meta-analysis are fair. The one on the meta-analysis confirms the survivorship and design concern about its four long-run studies.

There are weaker spots:
- The Summary conflates a change of hours measure with decay.
- The control arm was partly contaminated, which affects the decay estimate.
- The meetings figures don't reconcile with the meeting audit in two control offices.
- The log-hours measure is ambiguous in a way that matters for the mediation analysis.
- "Confirms" is too strong for a mediation result from 14 clusters, tested in the same offices that generated the hypothesis.

## 1. Arithmetic check

- **Per hour, timesheets:** 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098, so +9.8%. ✓
- **Per hour, system logs:** 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085, so +8.5%. ✓
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100. ✓
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, a fall of 13.4%. 0.968 / 0.866 = 1.118, so +11.8%. ✓
- **Counter staffing:** 0.83 × 1.12 × 1.067 ≈ 0.99, so 12% more staff would roughly restore baseline output. ✓
  - But then the cost per contact rises by about **12–13%**, not 9%. The 9% figure needs output about 3% above baseline, or a different reference point.
  - Utilisation would also fall with more staff, so restoring service might need more than 12%.
  - Please state the basis of the 9% estimate.

## 2. Main issues

**The Summary's decay figure mixes two measures.**
- "Fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months" compares a timesheet figure with a log-based figure.
- The like-for-like decline is 12.5% → 9.8% on timesheets, a fall of about a fifth. The body text and Section 5 get this right.
- The Summary should use the matched comparison.
- Separately, the two estimates have heavily overlapping CIs, and the difference is not tested. "Consistent with some fading" is the right phrasing; a formal test would help.

**Contamination in the control arm may explain part of the "decay".**
- Two of the seven control offices cut meetings in month 15. Their output per hour then rose 4.1% against their own previous period.
- If that held, the control arm's average rose by about 1.2 points (4.1 × 2/7). The treated-minus-control gap would narrow even if treated offices did not change at all.
- So some of the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may be control offices improving, not treated offices fading.
- A sensitivity analysis excluding those two offices, or excluding months 15–24 for them, would separate the two explanations. This matters, because decay is the claim most debated across the earlier documents.

**The meeting figures for control offices don't reconcile.**
- Control offices are reported as moving from 7.2 to 7.0 hours per week between baseline and month 24.
- But two of the seven cut from 7.1 to 5.0. That alone should lower the control mean by about 0.6 hours, to roughly 6.6.
- Either the other five control offices increased their meeting time, or the audit offices drifted back up, or the figures don't match. Please clarify.
- Related: the nine-month report said meeting data were collected only in month six, with no baseline. The baseline figures here (7.4 treated, 7.2 control) must come from historical calendar data. Say so. The balance at baseline is reassuring and worth reporting explicitly, since it answers the chance-imbalance concern.

**What do log hours measure?**
- "Active log-in time on the case-management system" sounds like time spent on cases. It may not include meetings, email, or other non-case work.
- If so, it is not a measure of total hours worked. Two consequences follow:
  - **The interpretation flips.** Log hours fell less than timesheet hours (11% vs 12%). That could simply mean meeting time was converted into case time, rather than revealing unclaimed work. The text reads it as "slightly more work than timesheets", which may be the wrong reading.
  - **The mediation analysis changes meaning.** If meetings are outside the denominator, then output per log hour rising because of fewer meetings needs an argument, such as less fragmented attention. If meetings are inside it, part of the meetings pathway is close to mechanical: removing non-output time raises output per hour by construction.
- Either reading is defensible, but the paper must say which one applies.

**The mediation result is supportive, not confirmatory.**
- **It is not an independent test.** The hypothesis came from the same seven treated offices. Registration at month 11 guards against choosing the model after seeing the outcome. It does not make this a replication in new units, which was the core of Varga & Holm's "won't replicate" objection.
- **Sample size.** "A larger sample of office-months" overstates the information. With 7 v 7 clusters, the effective sample is 14 offices. A 95% CI of 28–66% looks narrow for that.
  - How were the standard errors computed?
  - Was a small-cluster correction used, such as a wild cluster bootstrap?
- **Unmeasured confounding.** Acknowledged in the limitations, and real: managers who cut meetings may manage better in other ways too.
- **Correlated mediators.** Fewer meetings may also reduce fatigue. Splitting into 47% and 18% depends on how the joint pathway was allocated.
- So "confirms" in the Summary should become "supports".
- Even so, the result clearly answers the claim that the meetings explanation "should not be cited as a mechanism". It held up under a pre-specified test with baseline data.

## 3. Halden subset

- **Response bias:** only 14 of the 23 organisations with records responded. Non-responders plausibly include more that reverted or struggled. So 3 of 14 reverting (21%) is a *lower bound* on reversion among the 23.
- **The tidy categorisation is stretched.** The Summary says all three reverters had "client-facing or coverage obligations", but one is a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Marketing was one of Halden's discretionary sectors, so this reversion does not fit the coverage-bound pattern neatly. It deserves a sentence.
- **Framing:** treating the 11.8% as an upper bound for survivors twice over is exactly right.
- **The attrition question is unanswered.** Varga & Holm showed that seven of the nine Halden withdrawals came after the schedule began, contrary to the working paper's description. With a Halden author (Okafor) on this report, it is a natural place to correct or explain that.

## 4. Smaller points and outstanding requests

- **Backlog and case age** are still not reported. I asked for these at nine months as a check on easy-case prioritisation, and they matter more at 24 months.
- **Output per FTE drift:** −2.1% → −3.4%. Still not significant, but the trend is worth flagging.
- **Sick days (−27%):** still not expressed per scheduled day, so part of the fall may be mechanical.
- **Resignations:** reported without CIs.
- **Quality:** the appeal-overturn rate at 24 months (3.2% vs 3.0%) is now meaningful, because appeals have had time to work through. This is good evidence that quality held.
- **Ending the counter arm** is itself an informative result. Report it as such: a pre-specified outcome (waiting time) breached an operational threshold.
- **Unplanned audit:** the two-office observation is handled with appropriate caution. Regression to the mean and seasonality are additional reasons to discount the 4.1%.

## 5. Updated synthesis across all five documents

| Question | Best current evidence |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | About 8.5–10% at 24 months, randomised, against actual hours (log-based 8.5%, CI 3.4–13.8). Down from about 12.5% at 9 months, partly or wholly due to fading, with control contamination a possible contributor. |
| Output per employee, discretionary | About −2% to −3.5%, not significantly different from zero. |
| Coverage-bound work | Output per employee −9% to −11%. Service worsened enough that the county ended the arm at 12 months. |
| Headline 20%+ claims | Measurement artifacts: scheduled hours, manager reporting, survivorship. |
| "Entirely an artifact" | Not supported. |
| "No decay" | Not supported; there is modest decay. |
| Mechanism | Meeting reduction is the largest measured pathway (about half), fatigue is smaller (about a fifth), and about a third is unexplained. This is from one trial and still needs replication in new units. |
| Open question | Could reorganisation without cutting hours capture much of the gain? No study has tested this. It is the obvious next trial: randomise to hours cut vs meeting audit only vs control. |

I can draft a referee report on this follow-up, or turn the synthesis into a short policy brief.
